title: What does the evidence let us say?
subtitle: Evidence, inference, models, and prediction
paragraphs: Suppose I tell you that an object in space is approaching Earth. It is tempting to jump straight to a collision. But approaching Earth and hitting Earth are different claims. Before we predict what will happen, we need to separate what we know from what we think it means. That is where our work in physics begins.

Use evidence and inference in Section A to separate two claims. Evidence is what was observed, measured, or stated in the information we were given. An inference is a conclusion we draw from that evidence. An inference can be reasonable and still need testing. If we have a series of measured positions, those positions are evidence. Saying the object will continue along the same path is an inference that depends on an assumption about its motion.

A model makes that assumption clear. It is a simplified description that helps us explain a pattern and make a prediction we can test. Imagine a cart at 0 m, then 2 m, then 4 m, with one second between measurements. Its position increases by 2 m each second. If that pattern continues, we predict 6 m at 3 s. The prediction is not another measurement. In Section C, compare the dashed prediction with the measured dots. Blue identifies position; purple identifies the velocity pattern connecting the positions.

To predict a later position, we need a known starting position, a velocity with direction, and the time elapsed from that starting measurement. We also need to decide whether treating the velocity as constant is reasonable. With constant velocity, the model is <eq><var>x</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>x</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>v</var>Δ<var>t</var></eq>: final position equals initial position plus velocity times elapsed time. The velocity tells us how much position changes each second. Multiplying meters per second by seconds gives a change in meters.

Now test the pattern with the cart in Section D. Its positions are 10 m, 8 m, and 6 m at 0 s, 1 s, and 2 s. Position decreases by 2 m each second, so its velocity is −2 m/s. From the last measurement at 2 s to the requested time of 4 s, another 2 s pass. The predicted position is 6 m + (−2 m/s)(2 s) = 2 m. The negative sign tells us that position is decreasing along our chosen axis.

I want the reasoning and its limit to travel with that answer. Our claim is 2 m at 4 s. Our evidence is the measured pattern. Our reasoning extends that pattern for two more seconds. Our limit is the assumption that the velocity stays constant. A new reading of 3 m at 4 s would make us check the measurements and the model, including whether measurement uncertainty explains the difference or the motion changed.

This is how we will investigate our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ. A useful question is whether its predicted path reaches Earth's position at the same time Earth is there. We will build that prediction from measurements, explain our assumptions, and revise our conclusion when the evidence calls for it.

title: One trip can have several correct descriptions
subtitle: Position, distance, displacement, and reference frames
paragraphs: If I ask where you are, an answer like “two meters” leaves out something important: two meters from where? A position needs a reference frame. For motion along a straight line, we choose an origin, label it zero, and choose a positive direction. Once we agree on those choices, a position gives us a location we can interpret.

Suppose right is positive. A position of <eq><var>x</var> = −2 m</eq> means the object is two meters left of the origin. That sign describes location. It does not tell us which way the object is moving. An object at −2 m could move right, move left, or remain there. Keep location and motion separate as you read a situation.

Trace the two legs in Section C, starting at 0 m, traveling right to 4 m, and returning to 1 m. The distance traveled counts the entire route. The outward leg is 4 m and the return leg is 3 m, giving 7 m altogether. Returning does not erase distance already traveled. Distance is never negative because each leg contributes its length.

Use the displacement equation in Section B to ask a different question: how did position change from the start to the finish? The symbol Δ means “change in,” so Δx means change in position. We calculate final minus initial: Δx = xf − xi. For this trip, that is 1 m − 0 m = +1 m. The object finishes one meter to the right of where it began. The 7 m distance and +1 m displacement both describe this same trip.

This is also the difference between a scalar and a vector. A scalar has a magnitude and units; distance and elapsed time are examples. A vector also has direction. Displacement is a vector, and on our one-dimensional axis its sign communicates direction. In the diagram, the traveled path stays in pencil. The starting and finishing positions and the displacement arrow are blue because they describe position and its change.

The trip in Section D begins at −3 m, turns at +2 m, and finishes at −1 m. The first leg has length |2 − (−3)| = 5 m. The second has length |−1 − 2| = 3 m. The bars mean absolute value: we use the size of each position change when adding distance. Total distance is therefore 8 m. Displacement uses only the endpoints: −1 m − (−3 m) = +2 m.

Notice that the final position is negative while the displacement is positive. The object finishes left of the origin, but right of its starting position. If we reversed which direction we called positive, the coordinate signs would reverse. The physical trip and its distance would stay the same. I want your signs to communicate the reference frame you chose.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, we will need a clear origin, axes, and sign convention before a predicted position has meaning. Its total distance traveled tells us about the route. Its starting position and displacement tell us where it finishes. That distinction matters when we compare its predicted location with Earth's.

title: A graph can tell the story of motion
subtitle: Average velocity, speed, and position-time graphs
paragraphs: We can now describe where an object starts and finishes. The next question is how quickly its position changes. Moving four meters in two seconds and moving four meters in twenty seconds produce the same displacement, but they describe different motion. Time lets us tell the difference.

Use the ratio in Section B for average velocity: v̄ = Δx ÷ Δt. The bar means average over an interval. We use final minus initial for both changes. Velocity includes direction, so its sign depends on the axis we chose. Average speed uses total distance divided by elapsed time. Speed is nonnegative. When an object changes direction, average speed and the magnitude of average velocity can be different.

A position-time graph puts time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis. Every point identifies where the object is at a particular time. The graph's height gives position. Its slope, the vertical change divided by the horizontal change, gives velocity. The units show why: a change in meters divided by a change in seconds produces meters per second. This graph is a record of position over time, not a picture of the road's shape.

Trace the three segments of the position-time graph in Section C. From 0 s to 2 s, position rises from 0 m to 4 m. The slope is +4 m ÷ 2 s = +2 m/s. From 2 s to 4 s, position remains at 4 m. The horizontal line has zero slope, so the object is stopped. From 4 s to 6 s, it returns from 4 m to 0 m. The slope is −4 m ÷ 2 s = −2 m/s. It moves in the negative direction at a speed of 2 m/s. The purple marks connect each slope to its velocity.

Across that entire six-second trip, the object returns to its starting position. Its displacement is zero, so its average velocity is 0 m/s. It still travels 4 m out and 4 m back. Its average speed is 8 m ÷ 6 s ≈ 1.33 m/s. An average velocity of zero over the whole trip does not mean the object was stopped throughout it.

On a straight segment, the slope stays constant. A steeper segment means a larger speed because more position change occurs in the same time. A curved graph has a changing slope. Average velocity between two points uses the slope of the line joining them. Instantaneous velocity, the velocity at one moment, uses the slope of a tangent: a line that matches the curve's direction at that point.

In Section D, the straight line passes through (2 s, 14 m) and (6 s, 6 m). Velocity is (6 − 14) m ÷ (6 − 2) s = −2 m/s. If that velocity continues, two more seconds bring another −4 m of displacement. At 8 s the predicted position is 6 m + (−2 m/s)(2 s) = 2 m. Extending the straight line makes the same prediction.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, tracked positions and times let us estimate velocity along a chosen axis. I want the graph and calculation to tell the same story. We can then judge whether continuing with a constant-velocity prediction is reasonable or whether changing slopes call for a different model.

title: Velocity tells us more than speed
subtitle: Signed area, displacement, and velocity components
paragraphs: A velocity-time graph lets us recover a trip even when no positions are listed. The height tells us velocity at a particular time. To find displacement, we need to combine that velocity with how long it lasts. I want you to keep those two jobs separate: reading a height gives meters per second; finding an area gives meters.

For constant velocity, <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = <var>v</var>Δ<var>t</var></eq>. On the graph, that multiplication is the area of a rectangle: height times width. Above the time axis, velocity is positive and the area adds positive displacement. Below it, velocity is negative and the area adds negative displacement. This is signed area. The blue areas on your notes page represent changes in position, even though the vertical axis describes velocity.

Trace the two signed areas on the left of Section C. The cart travels at +3 m/s for 2 s, then −1 m/s for 2 s. Its first displacement is (+3 m/s)(2 s) = +6 m. Its second is (−1 m/s)(2 s) = −2 m. Combining them gives Δx = +6 m − 2 m = +4 m. The cart finishes four meters in the positive direction from where it started. That does not mean it traveled only four meters.

Check the two answers in Section D. Distance counts both legs by their lengths, so distance = 6 m + 2 m = 8 m. When a velocity graph crosses zero, split the areas there before adding their sizes for distance. A negative region does not undo travel already completed. A horizontal segment below zero also describes steady motion, not an object slowing down. Its velocity stays negative and its speed stays constant.

Velocity can also point at an angle. Then we describe the same motion using two perpendicular components, one along each axis. A component is a signed part of a vector. The object is not making two separate trips. Both components happen during the same interval and together describe the single velocity arrow.

On the right of Section C, the velocity has magnitude 10 m/s and points 30° from the positive horizontal axis toward the positive vertical axis. With that angle measured from the horizontal, vx = v cos θ and vy = v sin θ. Therefore vx = (10 m/s) cos 30° ≈ 8.66 m/s and vy = (10 m/s) sin 30° = 5.00 m/s. Both signs are positive because the arrow points toward increasing coordinates on both axes.

The angle's reference axis matters. Before choosing sine or cosine, identify which component is adjacent to that angle and which is opposite. Check the sketch as well as the calculator. Neither component should exceed the magnitude of the original vector. Purple identifies all three velocity arrows; the components explain the direction of the original arrow.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, motion toward Earth and motion across our line of sight both matter. One component alone cannot describe the entire path. Components let us predict each coordinate, while signed area keeps track of how motion along each axis changes position.

title: A prediction should carry its uncertainty
subtitle: Constant velocity, bounds, and a range of possible positions
paragraphs: A prediction written as one number can look more certain than the measurements supporting it. If our starting position is only known within a range, the predicted position should reflect that range. Today I want us to make both parts of a prediction visible: the central value and how far the allowed values could extend around it.

For steady velocity, xf = x0 + vt, where time is measured from the starting position. Suppose x0 = 8.0 ± 0.5 m, v = −2.0 ± 0.1 m/s, and the elapsed time is exactly 3 s in our model. The central prediction is xf = 8.0 m + (−2.0 m/s)(3 s) = 2.0 m. Position decreases because the velocity is negative.

Here the plus-or-minus amounts are bounds: limits on the values we allow. The starting position could lie anywhere from 7.5 m to 8.5 m, and the velocity from −2.1 m/s to −1.9 m/s. A more negative velocity produces a larger decrease in position during those three seconds. This is why keeping the signs matters when we find the endpoints.

Locate the two ends of the prediction interval in Section C. The lowest final position combines the lowest starting position with the most negative velocity: 7.5 m + (−2.1 m/s)(3 s) = 1.2 m. The highest combines the highest starting position with the least negative velocity: 8.5 m + (−1.9 m/s)(3 s) = 2.8 m. Every allowed combination falls between those limits, provided constant velocity and exact elapsed time remain valid assumptions.

Use the bound equation in Section B to check the width of that interval. Let δ mean the uncertainty bound on a quantity. For this model, δxf = δx0 + tδv. Thus δxf = 0.5 m + (3 s)(0.1 m/s) = 0.8 m. We report xf = 2.0 ± 0.8 m. The 0.8 m is the distance from the center to either limit. The full interval is 1.6 m wide.

Notice how velocity uncertainty grows into position uncertainty as time passes. An error of one tenth of a meter each second becomes three tenths of a meter after three seconds. The initial-position bound remains part of the result too. On the notes page, the central marker and surrounding blue interval show these two ideas without pretending that the center is an exact location.

These bounds are not a probability distribution or a statement that a certain percentage of results must fall inside the interval. We have added the largest allowed contributions. If time also had uncertainty, this expression would need revision. If the object accelerates, the constant-velocity model itself may fail, even when our arithmetic is correct.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a useful forecast includes the reference frame, future time, predicted range, and assumptions. New observations can narrow that range or reveal that the motion changed. Reporting uncertainty makes the claim more informative and gives us something specific to compare with the next measurement.

title: Add the directions before the lengths
subtitle: Vector components, resultants, and direction angles
paragraphs: Two trips do not combine the same way just because their lengths match. Walking four meters right and four meters left brings you back; walking both legs right does not. Direction must stay attached to displacement. Today we will use components to add vectors without losing that information.

Choose the positive horizontal axis toward east and the positive vertical axis toward north. A vector written as (6, −4) m means six meters in the positive horizontal direction and four meters in the negative vertical direction. These are signed components, not the vector's total length. Once the axes are chosen, every vector in the problem must use that same frame.

Keep the horizontal and vertical sums in Section B separate. Our first displacement is A = (6, −4) m, and the second is B = (−4, 8) m. Add matching components: Rx = Ax + Bx = 6 m − 4 m = 2 m and Ry = Ay + By = −4 m + 8 m = 4 m. The resultant is therefore R = (2, 4) m. It describes the overall displacement from the initial point to the final point.

Trace the tip-to-tail arrows in Section C, then trace the dashed resultant. The second arrow starts where the first ends. A single resultant arrow connects the original starting point to the final endpoint. Moving an arrow to build this diagram does not change its length or direction. Reversing the order of the two displacements changes the intermediate point, but their final vector sum stays the same.

To find the resultant's magnitude, use the right triangle formed by its perpendicular components: <eq><var>R</var> = √(<var>R</var><sub>x</sub>² + <var>R</var><sub>y</sub>²)</eq>. Here <eq><var>R</var> = √[(2 m)² + (4 m)²] = √20 m ≈ 4.47 m</eq>. Magnitude is nonnegative. Adding the individual vector magnitudes instead would describe the total length of the two-leg route, not the size of the resultant displacement.

The direction needs an angle and a reference axis. Both resultant components are positive, so the arrow lies in the upper-right quadrant. From the positive horizontal axis, <eq>tan <var>θ</var> = <var>R</var><sub>y</sub> ÷ <var>R</var><sub>x</sub> = 4 ÷ 2 = 2</eq>, giving <eq><var>θ</var> ≈ 63.4°</eq>. That is 63.4° toward north from east. Saying only “63.4 degrees” would leave the direction incomplete.

I want you to check the quadrant before trusting an inverse-tangent answer. The same ratio can occur when both components are negative, even though that arrow points the opposite way. A sketch and signed components resolve the ambiguity. The resultant here should lean more upward than rightward because its vertical component is larger.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, component addition lets us combine changes in motion while preserving direction. A large sideways component can matter as much as a component toward Earth. The calculation and the arrow diagram should identify the same final direction, not just produce a plausible-looking number.

title: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing
subtitle: Velocity changes, graph slopes, and a turning point
paragraphs: Imagine a cart moving right while a steady influence changes its velocity toward the left. At first the cart slows down. Later it may stop and begin moving left faster and faster. The acceleration can remain the same through that entire story. I want us to describe what changes without letting a negative sign stand in for an explanation.

Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity: <eq><var>a</var><sub>avg</sub> = Δ<var>v</var> ÷ Δ<var>t</var></eq>. Its units are meters per second each second, written m/s². A negative acceleration means the velocity changes in the negative direction on our chosen axis. Whether speed increases or decreases depends on the velocity the object already has.

Take right as positive. In Section D, velocity changes from +6 m/s to −2 m/s in 4 s. The change is Δv = −2 m/s − (+6 m/s) = −8 m/s. Therefore aavg = −8 m/s ÷ 4 s = −2 m/s². We are told the acceleration is constant, so this average also describes the acceleration at each moment in the interval.

Constant acceleration gives <eq><var>v</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>a</var><var>t</var></eq>. Each second, the cart's velocity decreases by 2 m/s. Starting at +6 m/s, it reaches +4, then +2, then 0, then −2 m/s at successive whole seconds. On the velocity-time graph, these values lie on a straight line. Its slope is negative because velocity decreases as time increases.

Find where the line in Section C crosses the time axis. That is the turning point. Setting 0 m/s = 6 m/s + (−2 m/s²)t gives t = 3 s. During those first three seconds, velocity is positive and acceleration is negative, so speed decreases. During the next second, both are negative, so the cart speeds up in the negative direction. The red and green regions on the notes page mark that change in speed behavior.

At the exact turning instant, the cart's velocity is zero, but its acceleration is still −2 m/s². An object can be momentarily stopped while its velocity is changing. If acceleration also vanished and stayed zero at that moment, it would remain stopped. That is a different physical situation, and we should not assume it just because the velocity passes through zero.

This gives us a useful one-dimensional check. When nonzero velocity and acceleration have the same sign, speed increases. When they have opposite signs, speed decreases. The graph's slope tells us acceleration; the graph's height tells us velocity. A downward-sloping line may describe slowing on one part of the graph and speeding up on another.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, gravity can change velocity rather than simply maintain it. The direction of that change matters. Before deciding whether the asteroid is speeding up, slowing down, or changing its path, we need both its existing velocity and its acceleration. A signed answer is useful only when we can explain the motion it describes.

title: Choose the equation that fits the information
subtitle: Constant acceleration, stopping distance, and independent checks
paragraphs: When a problem gives several numbers, it is tempting to search for an equation and start substituting. I want you to pause first. Name the starting and ending conditions, choose a positive direction, and identify the quantity you need. An equation is a statement about a model. Choosing one should follow from the information and assumptions in the situation.

Our car begins moving in the positive direction at 20 m/s and brakes with constant acceleration −4 m/s² until it stops. The final velocity is 0 m/s. We need stopping displacement, and time has not been given. Find the row marked “time” in the Omits column of Section B. The relation vf² = vi² + 2aΔx connects exactly those quantities without requiring time.

Substitute the signed values: <eq>(0 m/s)² = (20 m/s)² + 2(−4 m/s²)Δ<var>x</var></eq>. Rearranging gives <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = [(0 m/s)² − (20 m/s)²] ÷ [2(−4 m/s²)] = 50 m</eq>. Both numerator and denominator are negative, so displacement is positive. The units reduce to meters. Those signs tell a consistent story: the car moves forward while its forward velocity decreases.

Now find the time using <eq><var>v</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>a</var><var>t</var></eq>. Rearranging gives <eq><var>t</var> = (0 − 20) m/s ÷ (−4 m/s²) = 5 s</eq>. Negative acceleration does not require negative time or displacement. It describes the change in velocity. We stop the model at five seconds because the question asks for the first stop, not continued motion in reverse.

Trace the triangle in Section C to check the stopping distance from Section D. Constant acceleration makes velocity fall along a straight line from 20 m/s to zero. The area between that line and the time axis is a triangle: Δx = ½(5 s)(20 m/s) = 50 m. The entire area is above zero, so displacement is positive. Because the car never reverses during this interval, its distance traveled is also 50 m.

The average of the endpoint velocities works here because acceleration is constant: <eq><var>v</var><sub>avg</sub> = (20 + 0) m/s ÷ 2 = 10 m/s</eq>. Multiplying that average by five seconds gives the same displacement. Equivalently, <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = ½(<var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>v</var><sub>f</sub>)<var>t</var></eq>. If initial velocity, acceleration, and time were given instead, <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub><var>t</var> + ½<var>a</var><var>t</var>²</eq> would be convenient.

These equations describe the same constant-acceleration model from different sets of information. They are not permission to assume constant acceleration whenever numbers are available. If braking changes during the stop, we would need more information, a graph, or a model divided into appropriate intervals.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, we must make the same decision before predicting a new position. Can velocity reasonably stay constant, or must its change be included? I want the chosen equation, signed calculation, units, and graph to support one physical story, with the model's limits stated alongside it.

title: Balanced forces can go with steady motion
subtitle: Newton's first law, inertia, and equilibrium
paragraphs: A book sliding across a table eventually stops. That everyday observation can make it seem as if motion needs a continuing forward force. But the book is also interacting with the table and the air. To understand why its motion changes, we need to identify those interactions rather than assume stopping is what all moving objects naturally do.

Newton's first law says that an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity when the net external force on it is zero, viewed from an inertial frame. An inertial frame is a nonaccelerating reference frame in which this law holds. For our classroom examples, we treat the room as such a frame. Constant velocity means both speed and direction stay unchanged.

The net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on the chosen object. Individual forces can be present while their sum is zero. Compare the horizontal arrows on the cart in Section C. Here 8 N right balances 8 N left. The upward and downward forces balance too. Thus ΣF = 0 and a = 0. The symbol Σ means add all the relevant forces, including their directions.

Zero acceleration tells us velocity does not change. It does not tell us that velocity is zero. Suppose the cart is already moving at +3 m/s. With balanced forces, it continues at +3 m/s. If that same balanced-force situation began with the cart at rest, it would remain at rest. We need the initial velocity to distinguish those two cases.

The example in Section D starts the cart at −2 m and keeps the forces balanced for 4 s. Its displacement is Δx = (3 m/s)(4 s) = +12 m. Using xf = x0 + vt, we obtain xf = −2 m + 12 m = 10 m. The cart changes position even though its acceleration and net force are zero.

We call the resistance to a change in velocity inertia. It is a property of matter, not an extra force that should be drawn pushing the cart forward. Mass measures inertia: a larger mass requires a larger net force to produce the same acceleration. In the balanced situation, however, neither a small nor a large mass accelerates just because it is moving.

The vocabulary in Section A calls this balance equilibrium. It can describe rest or steady straight-line motion. The yellow code on the notes page marks that balance; purple identifies velocity. Keeping those ideas separate also explains the sliding book. Friction supplies a force opposing its sliding motion, so the horizontal forces do not balance and its velocity changes. A continuing push can maintain steady motion when it balances that friction.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, motion through space does not require a forward force to keep it going. Gravity can still provide a net force and change its velocity, including its direction. I want us to ask what forces change the motion, then use the existing velocity to explain what the object actually does.

title: Every force has a source and a receiver
subtitle: Weight, normal force, tension, and supported objects
paragraphs: Before we add forces, we need to know which forces belong in the calculation. A useful habit is to name both the object receiving a force and the object exerting it. “The rope pulls on the crate” identifies an interaction. “The crate is moving” describes its motion, but does not identify a new force. I want each arrow to have a physical source.

Weight is the gravitational force Earth exerts on an object. Near Earth's surface, its magnitude is <eq><var>W</var> = <var>m</var><var>g</var></eq>. Mass is measured in kilograms; weight is measured in newtons. We use <eq><var>g</var> = 9.8 N/kg</eq>, meaning each kilogram has 9.8 N of gravitational force acting on it in this model. The same value can be expressed as 9.8 m/s² when describing free-fall acceleration.

The normal force comes from contact with a surface and acts perpendicular to that surface. Tension comes from a taut rope and pulls along the rope, away from the object. Neither force is automatically equal to weight. Its magnitude depends on the other forces and on the object's acceleration. A surface and a rope can share the job of supporting an object.

Follow the given values in Section D for the 3 kg crate resting on a level table while a vertical rope pulls upward with 10 N. Earth's downward pull is W = (3 kg)(9.8 N/kg) = 29.4 N. The table pushes upward with a normal force whose magnitude we have not yet found. There are three forces on the crate: weight, tension, and the normal force.

The crate stays at rest, so its vertical acceleration is zero. Choose upward as positive. The force equation is <eq><var>N</var> + <var>T</var> − <var>W</var> = 0</eq>. Substituting gives <eq><var>N</var> + 10 N − 29.4 N = 0</eq>, so <eq><var>N</var> = 19.4 N</eq>. Here italic N represents the normal-force magnitude; upright N after a number is the unit newton. The rope supplies part of the upward support, leaving the table to supply the rest.

Trace each of the three arrows in Section C back to its named source. The crate receives all three forces. Orange identifies force. If the arrows use one consistent scale, the two upward lengths together should match the downward length. The normal arrow should be longer than the tension arrow, but shorter than the weight arrow. That picture is a useful check on the numbers and the balance equation.

If the rope were absent and the crate remained at rest, the normal force would equal the weight. That equality follows from the particular situation; it is not the definition of a normal force. An inclined surface or an additional vertical force changes the calculation. Likewise, mass remains the same when support changes, even though a scale's reading can change.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, we will name the source of every proposed force before using it. Gravity can act without contact. A rope, supporting surface, or engine force belongs only when that interaction exists. A clear list of sources and receivers prevents us from inventing forces simply to match the motion we expect.

title: The same force can produce different accelerations
subtitle: Total moving mass, inverse relationships, and experimental controls
paragraphs: Suppose I use the same net force to accelerate two carts, but one carries more mass. The heavier system changes velocity more slowly. That comparison is useful only if the net force really stays the same. Today we are looking at how acceleration depends on mass while holding the force constant, and how a graph can make that relationship visible.

Newton's second law connects the quantities: <eq><var>F</var><sub>net</sub> = <var>M</var><var>a</var></eq>, or <eq><var>a</var> = <var>F</var><sub>net</sub> ÷ <var>M</var></eq>. Here the capital M means the total mass of the system we are accelerating. In a cart-and-hanger arrangement, the hanger's mass belongs in that total if it moves as part of our chosen system. Counting only the cart would make our model incomplete.

Compare the mass and acceleration columns in Section C. They show 1 kg accelerating at 4 m/s² and 2 kg accelerating at 2 m/s². Each trial gives the same product: (1 kg)(4 m/s²) = (2 kg)(2 m/s²) = 4 N. That common product is the net force. Doubling mass halves acceleration when the net force is unchanged.

Use the mass in Section D for the next prediction. For a 3 kg system under that same net force, a = 4 N ÷ 3 kg ≈ 1.33 m/s². For 4 kg, the acceleration would be 1 m/s². These values form an inverse relationship. Equal additions of mass do not produce equal decreases in acceleration. The graph of acceleration against mass therefore bends instead of forming a straight line.

We can reveal the pattern by plotting acceleration against reciprocal mass, meaning one divided by mass. The equation becomes <eq><var>a</var> = <var>F</var><sub>net</sub>(1/<var>M</var>)</eq>. This graph is a straight line through the origin for the ideal model. Its slope is the fixed net force. The horizontal units are inverse kilograms, and dividing m/s² by inverse kilograms gives kg·m/s², or newtons.

That graph is more than a way to make the data look tidy. It tests a specific prediction: acceleration should be proportional to reciprocal mass under constant net force. If the data do not follow the predicted line within measurement uncertainty, we should examine the setup and assumptions. Friction, a changing pull, or an incorrectly counted moving mass can change the relationship we actually measured.

I want us to distinguish a controlled variable from something we merely hope stayed constant. Adding mass may also change friction. Moving mass between a cart and a hanger may preserve total mass while changing the driving force. The force diagram and system boundary help us decide whether two trials truly test the same relationship. Orange represents the applied forces; the measured change in velocity supplies acceleration.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a fixed proposed push would produce less acceleration for a larger mass. But this does not mean more massive objects automatically fall more slowly under gravity. Gravitational force also depends on mass. We must check what is held constant before carrying a relationship from one physical situation into another.

title: An applied pull is not always the net force
subtitle: Fixed mass, friction, and force-acceleration graphs
paragraphs: If we double a pulling force, will acceleration double? It can, but only when the net force doubles and the mass stays fixed. The force we apply may have to overcome another force acting in the opposite direction. Today I want us to keep the applied force and the sum of all forces separate from the start.

Our model is a 2 kg object sliding in the positive horizontal direction. Friction acts backward with a constant magnitude of 0.4 N. The vertical forces balance. Horizontally, Fnet = Fdrive − f, and Newton's second law gives a = Fnet ÷ M. The signs describe the forces along our chosen axis.

Start with the first driving force in Section D. With a 2 N driving force, the net force is Fnet = 2.0 N − 0.4 N = 1.6 N. Therefore a = 1.6 N ÷ 2 kg = 0.8 m/s². The backward friction force reduces the velocity change produced each second, but the net force is still forward, so acceleration is positive.

Now increase the drive to 4 N while keeping the mass and sliding-friction model unchanged. The net force becomes Fnet = 4.0 N − 0.4 N = 3.6 N, and a = 3.6 N ÷ 2 kg = 1.8 m/s². The drive doubled, but acceleration changed from 0.8 to 1.8 m/s². It did not merely double to 1.6 m/s² because the net force did not merely double.

Plotting acceleration against net force produces a straight line through the origin for fixed mass. Its slope is <eq>1/<var>M</var> = 1/(2 kg) = 0.5 kg⁻¹</eq>. Each extra newton of net force adds 0.5 m/s² of acceleration. The graph gives another way to estimate mass: a larger mass produces a shallower acceleration-versus-net-force slope.

Compare the solid and dashed lines in Section C. Plotting against the driving force still gives a straight line in this sliding model, but it is shifted by friction. The equation is a = (Fdrive − f)/M. Its mathematical acceleration intercept is negative because friction is being subtracted. We should not extend that line blindly to an object resting on the table: static friction behaves differently, and the direction of sliding matters too.

The experimental question is whether mass and opposing forces stayed consistent across trials. If we change the hanger, load, or surface, we may change more than the intended driving force. In the notes diagram, compare the orange force arrows before interpreting the acceleration values. The difference between the forward and backward arrows is what enters Newton's second law.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a proposed engine or push would be one interaction in a larger force picture. We would add it to gravity and any other relevant forces to find the net change. I want our prediction to follow from that complete sum, with the mass and model assumptions stated clearly.

title: The force tells us how motion changes
subtitle: Net force, acceleration, and a cart moving the other way
paragraphs: A force arrow pointing right does not guarantee that the object is moving right. It tells us about an interaction. The net force determines acceleration, and acceleration tells us how velocity changes. To describe the motion itself, we also need the velocity the object already has. Today we will follow that chain carefully.

Choose right as positive. Our 4 kg cart has a 12 N force to the right and a 4 N force to the left. Both forces act on the cart, so they belong in the same horizontal sum: ΣFx = 12 N − 4 N = +8 N. Using only the larger force would ignore a real interaction. Adding both magnitudes without signs would ignore their opposite directions.

Use the force sum in Section B with right as positive: ΣFx = max. Thus ax = +8 N ÷ 4 kg = +2 m/s². The acceleration points right, matching the net force. The vertical forces are balanced, so they produce no vertical acceleration and do not add to the horizontal force sum.

Now include the starting velocity, −3 m/s. The cart initially moves left. With constant forces and mass, acceleration remains constant, so after 1 s we use vf = vi + axt. Substitution gives vf = −3 m/s + (2 m/s²)(1 s) = −1 m/s. The cart still moves left, but its speed has fallen from 3 m/s to 1 m/s.

This is what positive acceleration means here: the signed velocity becomes more positive by 2 m/s each second. It does not instantly become positive. From −3 to −1 is an increase in velocity but a decrease in speed. I want you to say both parts when interpreting the answer, because the sign and the size describe different features of the motion.

If the same forces continue, the cart reaches zero velocity after <eq><var>t</var> = (0 − (−3)) m/s ÷ (2 m/s²) = 1.5 s</eq>. It then moves right and speeds up. There is no need for the net force to reverse at the turning point. The same rightward acceleration first slows the leftward motion and then builds rightward motion.

In Section C, compare the cart’s force and velocity arrows. The orange arrows identify forces and the purple arrow identifies initial velocity. The red label applies to the first second because speed decreases during that interval. The net-force arrow is a summary of the force sum, shown separately; it is not an additional force to add again. Keeping the picture and calculation connected helps prevent double-counting.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a force toward Earth tells us the direction of its acceleration due to that interaction. Its existing velocity might have components toward, away from, or across that direction. A useful forecast combines the net force with that initial motion and an elapsed time, rather than assuming the asteroid immediately travels along the force arrow.

title: Equal forces can have unequal effects
subtitle: Newton's third law, separate objects, and system boundaries
paragraphs: When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other. That statement applies even when one object is much larger or appears to do most of the moving. Newton's third law describes the two forces in a single interaction: they have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, and they act at the same time on different objects.

Read the object names on either side of the equation in Section B: FA on B = −FB on A. The labels matter as much as the minus sign. One force is received by B; the other is received by A. The force on B does not belong in A's individual force sum. I want us to identify the receivers before deciding whether two arrows can cancel in a calculation.

Our example has cart A with mass 1 kg and cart B with mass 3 kg. Their interaction pushes A left with 6 N and B right with 6 N. Take right as positive and assume no other horizontal forces. For A, aA = −6 N ÷ 1 kg = −6 m/s². For B, aB = +6 N ÷ 3 kg = +2 m/s².

The forces are equal in magnitude, but A's acceleration has three times B's magnitude. The smaller mass undergoes a larger velocity change each second under the same force size. That difference does not violate the third law. The third law compares the interaction forces; the second law explains how each object's mass responds to its own net force.

Find the receiver of each force in Section C. The diagram uses two equal-length orange arrows pointing opposite ways. A separate force diagram for A includes the leftward force on A. A separate diagram for B includes the rightward force on B. If we put both arrows on one cart merely because they form a pair, we would incorrectly predict no acceleration for that cart.

We can instead choose the combined A-and-B system. Then this interaction is internal: both members of the pair act between parts inside our chosen boundary. Their contributions cancel in the combined system's net external-force calculation. The carts can still accelerate relative to one another. With no external horizontal force, the combined system's center-of-mass velocity stays constant.

A third-law pair is not just any two opposite forces of equal size. Weight and a table's normal force on a resting book both act on the book, so they are not partners. The partner of Earth's pull on the book is the book's pull on Earth. The partner of the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table. Naming sources and receivers makes the distinction clear.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, Earth pulls on the asteroid and the asteroid pulls on Earth with equal force magnitudes at the same instant. Their very different masses produce very different accelerations. Earth's pull belongs in the asteroid's force diagram; the asteroid's pull on Earth does not cancel it there. Our system boundary determines which forces enter each prediction.

title: A force diagram begins with one chosen object
subtitle: External interactions, scaled arrows, and an accelerating lamp
paragraphs: A useful force diagram leaves out many visible details so that the interactions become easier to see. The first decision is the object or system we are studying. Every force arrow in that diagram must act on that chosen receiver. Today I want us to draw that boundary before writing Newton's second law.

Consider a 2 kg lamp hanging from a taut vertical rope. The lamp accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s². We choose the lamp as our object. The rope exerts upward tension on it, and Earth exerts downward weight. Those are the two external forces in this model. The force the lamp exerts on the rope belongs on the rope's diagram, not on the lamp's.

Use the positive direction in Section B, upward. The lamp's weight magnitude is W = mg = (2 kg)(9.8 m/s²) = 19.6 N. Because weight acts downward, it enters the vertical sum with a minus sign. Tension acts upward and enters with a plus sign. Newton's second law becomes T − mg = may.

Rearranging gives <eq><var>T</var> = <var>m</var><var>g</var> + <var>m</var><var>a</var><sub>y</sub></eq>. Substituting, <eq><var>T</var> = 19.6 N + (2 kg)(1.5 m/s²) = 22.6 N</eq>. The rope must supply enough upward force to balance the weight and an additional 3.0 N to produce the upward acceleration. The net force is therefore 3.0 N upward, not 22.6 N.

Compare the lengths of the two force arrows in Section C. Draw the upward tension arrow longer than the downward weight arrow, using the same length scale for both. Their difference represents the net force. A separately labeled net-force arrow can summarize the calculation, but it is not a third interaction to add to tension and weight. Adding it again would count the same imbalance twice.

Tension and weight are not a third-law pair. They both act on the lamp, come from different sources, and here even have different magnitudes. The tension's partner is the lamp's pull on the rope. The weight's partner is the lamp's gravitational pull on Earth. Neither partner belongs in this single-object diagram.

An upward acceleration also does not, by itself, prove that the lamp is moving upward. It could be moving downward and slowing. If it is already moving upward, it speeds up. The forces determine the change in velocity; a starting velocity is still needed to determine the motion. Any velocity arrow should be kept distinct from the orange force arrows so it cannot be mistaken for another force.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, we will use exactly this discipline. Define the asteroid as the receiver, list the external interactions on it, and draw their directions before combining them. An uncluttered diagram is useful because it makes missing forces, incorrect receivers, and double-counted components easier to catch before they affect the forecast.

title: Choose axes that help explain the ramp
subtitle: Inclined surfaces, weight components, and normal force
paragraphs: A block on a ramp still has weight acting straight down, but its motion follows the slope. We can choose axes that make that motion easier to describe. Let the parallel axis point downhill and the perpendicular axis point outward from the surface. Rotating our axes does not change any physical force. It changes how we describe the force's components.

Our 2 kg block slides down a ramp inclined 30° above horizontal. Friction acts uphill with magnitude 2 N. The actual forces are weight downward, normal force perpendicular away from the ramp, and friction along the ramp. With g = 9.8 m/s², the weight magnitude is W = mg = 19.6 N.

Match each component in Section B to an axis along or perpendicular to the ramp. Its downhill component has magnitude Wparallel = mg sin θ, while its component into the surface has magnitude Winto = mg cos θ. The ramp angle determines this component triangle. A useful check is a nearly level ramp: the downhill component should approach zero, while nearly all the weight points into the surface.

For our angle, the downhill part is <eq>(19.6 N) sin 30° = 9.8 N</eq>. Friction opposes it, so <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>parallel</sub> = 9.8 N − 2.0 N = 7.8 N</eq>. Newton's second law then gives <eq><var>a</var><sub>parallel</sub> = 7.8 N ÷ 2 kg = 3.9 m/s²</eq> downhill. Because the block is already sliding downhill, this acceleration makes it speed up.

The block does not accelerate through the solid ramp or away from it in this model. Its perpendicular acceleration is zero. Taking outward as positive gives <eq><var>N</var> − <var>m</var><var>g</var> cos <var>θ</var> = 0</eq>, so <eq><var>N</var> = (19.6 N) cos 30° ≈ 17.0 N</eq>. This normal force is smaller than the total weight. It balances only the component pressing into the ramp.

That normal-force equation depends on the situation. It works because there are no other perpendicular forces and no perpendicular acceleration. An angled pull or a curved surface could change the calculation. I want you to begin with the force balance instead of assuming normal force always equals either weight or one memorized expression.

Compare the two views in Section C. The drawing separates the actual-force diagram from the weight-component triangle. This distinction prevents a common mistake: adding weight and then adding both of its components as if three separate interactions existed. The components replace weight in the calculation; they do not supplement it. Orange marks force information in both views, while the ramp and axes remain in pencil.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, useful axes might follow a proposed path or point toward a gravitational source. Whatever axes we choose, the resulting prediction should describe the same physical motion. Components make the mathematics manageable, but the real interactions and the chosen system must remain consistent throughout the calculation.

title: Friction changes when slipping begins
subtitle: Adjustable static friction and the kinetic-friction model
paragraphs: If I push gently on a heavy box and it stays still, friction has matched my push. Pushing a little harder can make friction grow while the box remains at rest. That behavior shows why we cannot assign one fixed friction force to every situation. We first need to decide whether the surfaces are slipping relative to each other.

Static friction prevents relative slipping when it can. Its magnitude adjusts from zero up to a limit: <eq>0 ≤ <var>f</var><sub>s</sub> ≤ <var>μ</var><sub>s</sub><var>N</var></eq>. The coefficient μ is dimensionless, and the subscript s identifies the static case. The product of the coefficient and normal force gives the maximum available static friction, not necessarily the friction currently acting.

Our box has mass 2 kg on a level surface, with a horizontal pull and no vertical acceleration. Therefore N = mg = (2 kg)(9.8 m/s²) = 19.6 N. With μs = 0.40, the static limit is fs,max = (0.40)(19.6 N) = 7.84 N. We find the normal force first because another vertical force would change this limit.

Use the static-friction limit in Section B to check this case. Pull horizontally with 6 N while the box is at rest. Static friction can supply 6 N in the opposite direction because that is below its 7.84 N limit. The net force is 6 N − 6 N = 0 N, so acceleration is zero. Using 7.84 N as the actual friction here would falsely predict a backward acceleration from a gentle forward push.

Once the box slides, we use the kinetic-friction model fk = μkN. With μk = 0.25, its magnitude is fk = (0.25)(19.6 N) = 4.90 N. For a 10 N pull in the direction of sliding, Fnet = 10 N − 4.90 N = 5.10 N, giving a = 5.10 N ÷ 2 kg = 2.55 m/s² forward.

Trace the rising segment in Section C up to the slip threshold. It shows static friction rising with the pull until the limit, followed by a lower kinetic-friction level once sliding occurs. That level is constant in our simplified model because the normal force and kinetic coefficient stay constant. Real surfaces can behave more complicatedly, but this distinction between adjusting static friction and modeled sliding friction is the starting point.

Friction opposes relative slipping, or the tendency to slip, at the contact. It does not always oppose an object's overall motion in every situation. A shoe pushing backward on the ground can receive forward static friction that helps a person walk. I want the contact and its slipping tendency identified before we choose the arrow's direction.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, empty space does not provide a surface that continually applies sliding friction. Gravity can still change its velocity, and atmospheric drag would matter inside an atmosphere. Naming the actual interaction keeps our forecast from including a familiar force where its physical source is absent.

title: Balance each direction, not just the force sizes
subtitle: Equilibrium, angled ropes, and component sums
paragraphs: A hanging sign can be supported by two ropes, yet each rope may need more tension than half the sign's weight. The reason is direction. An angled rope supplies both a horizontal and a vertical force component. Only its vertical part supports the weight. Today I want us to make that geometry part of the force balance.

Equilibrium means acceleration is zero. In two dimensions, both component sums must vanish: <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>x</sub> = 0</eq> and <eq>Σ<var>F</var><sub>y</sub> = 0</eq>. This can describe an object remaining at rest or moving with constant velocity. Merely observing zero velocity at one instant is not enough; an object at a turning point can be stopped momentarily while accelerating.

Our sign weighs 40 N and remains at rest. It hangs from two ropes arranged symmetrically, each 30° above horizontal. Equal angles and symmetric loading give equal tension magnitudes. The left rope pulls upward and left; the right rope pulls upward and right. Both are actual forces on the sign, along with Earth's downward gravitational force.

Use the angle marked in Section C. For each rope, the horizontal component has magnitude Tx = T cos 30°. Those components point opposite ways and cancel. The vertical component of each rope is Ty = T sin 30°. Both point upward, so they add. The vertical balance becomes 2T sin 30° − 40 N = 0.

Since the sine of 30° is one half, <eq>2<var>T</var>(0.5) = 40 N</eq>, giving <eq><var>T</var> = 40 N</eq> in each rope. Each rope contributes <eq>(40 N) sin 30° = 20 N</eq> upward. The two upward components support the 40 N weight. A claim of 20 N tension per rope would confuse the vertical component with the full tension along the rope.

Check the vertical sum in Section B against the two vertical arrows in Section C. The orange diagonal arrows show the full tensions; the vertical parts show their contributions to support. We must not add each full tension and then add its components again. The component picture is another description of the same force. As with the ramp, it is a calculation tool rather than a set of extra interactions.

The angle is measured above horizontal, which is why sine gives the vertical part. If the angle were measured from vertical, cosine would give that part instead. The physical result cannot depend on how we label the angle. More nearly horizontal ropes need greater tension to supply the same vertical support, because each newton along the rope contributes less upward force. Perfectly horizontal ropes could not support this weight with any finite tension in this ideal model.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, zero net force would mean its velocity stays constant, not that it necessarily stops. We would need to check every coordinate direction before making that claim. I want a balance calculation to include the components, their signs, and the reason equilibrium is justified, rather than relying on equal-looking arrows alone.

title: Find the first step that changes the story
subtitle: Repairing force sums, signs, and interpretations
paragraphs: When two solutions disagree, finding a different final number is not enough. We need to locate the first step where the reasoning stops matching the physical situation. A later calculation can be perfectly executed and still carry forward an earlier mistake. Today I want us to explain the repair, not just replace an answer.

Start by naming the quantity being found and the reference frame. Position, displacement, velocity, speed, and acceleration answer different questions. Their units also differ. A number can have the right sign for position and the wrong interpretation for velocity. Keeping the quantity's name beside the number is a simple way to make the reasoning visible.

In the force example in Section D, a 3 kg cart experiences 9 N right and 3 N left. Someone divides the larger force by mass and reports 3 m/s². The first error is selecting the force, not performing the division. Newton's second law uses the net force on the object. With right positive, ΣFx = 9 N − 3 N = +6 N.

The corrected acceleration is <eq><var>a</var><sub>x</sub> = +6 N ÷ 3 kg = +2 m/s²</eq>. Check it by multiplying mass and acceleration: <eq>(3 kg)(2 m/s²) = 6 N</eq>, which matches the force sum. The unit check works because a newton is a kilogram-meter per second squared, so newtons divided by kilograms give m/s². The force diagram also shows a rightward imbalance, matching the acceleration sign.

Trace the line from left to right in Section C. Decide whether its change in height is positive or negative. Velocity changes from −2 m/s to −6 m/s in 2 s. Final minus initial gives Δv = −6 m/s − (−2 m/s) = −4 m/s. Subtracting a negative adds its positive counterpart; it does not make the final result automatically positive. Therefore aavg = −4 m/s ÷ 2 s = −2 m/s².

That negative acceleration goes with increasing speed in this interval. The object moves in the negative direction throughout, while speed grows from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. The downward slope of the velocity graph means velocity becomes more negative. It does not mean the object is slowing. Purple identifies signed velocity, and green marks the increasing speed.

A useful check should examine the reasoning from another angle. Compare a calculation with a graph, inspect whether all forces were included, or test whether the units and limiting behavior make sense. Repeating the same mistaken substitution in another equation may reproduce the same error. If one step changes, follow that correction through every result that depends on it.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, an incorrect starting coordinate, force sum, or sign can shift an entire forecast. Before sharing a prediction, we should trace it back through the measurements, chosen frame, and assumptions. An explanation of the first wrong step makes the correction understandable and shows why the revised conclusion deserves more confidence.

title: Follow the chain from force to position
subtitle: Constant net force, velocity reversal, and signed displacement
paragraphs: We now have the pieces needed to predict motion from forces. The net force gives acceleration. Acceleration changes velocity. Velocity over time changes position. I want each link to use the same object, reference frame, and time interval. That consistency matters especially when an object reverses direction during the calculation.

Start with the given values in Section D. Our 2 kg cart starts at 1 m with velocity −2 m/s. A constant net force of +4 N acts for 3 s. Take right as positive. The first step is a = ΣF ÷ m = 4 N ÷ 2 kg = +2 m/s². Because force and mass stay constant, acceleration stays constant over the interval.

Next find final velocity: <eq><var>v</var><sub>f</sub> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub> + <var>a</var><var>t</var> = −2 m/s + (2 m/s²)(3 s) = +4 m/s</eq>. The cart began moving left and finishes moving right. Its velocity passes through zero at <eq><var>t</var> = (0 − (−2)) m/s ÷ (2 m/s²) = 1 s</eq>. Positive acceleration first slows the negative motion, then builds positive motion.

The displacement equation covers the entire constant-acceleration interval, including the turn: <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = <var>v</var><sub>i</sub><var>t</var> + ½<var>a</var><var>t</var>²</eq>. Substitution gives <eq>Δ<var>x</var> = (−2 m/s)(3 s) + ½(2 m/s²)(3 s)² = −6 m + 9 m = +3 m</eq>. Finally add the starting coordinate: <eq><var>x</var><sub>f</sub> = 1 m + 3 m = 4 m</eq>. Displacement and final position are different quantities.

Compare the areas below and above the time axis in Section C. Their signed sum explains why displacement is only 3 m. During the first second, the velocity line lies below zero. Its triangular area is −½(1 s)(2 m/s) = −1 m. During the next two seconds, the line lies above zero, giving +½(2 s)(4 m/s) = +4 m. Adding the signed areas gives the same +3 m displacement. The blue regions track position change; the purple line tracks velocity.

Distance uses the sizes of those two regions instead: <eq>distance = 1 m + 4 m = 5 m</eq>. The cart travels from its starting coordinate of 1 m leftward to 0 m, then rightward to 4 m. That route makes the distinction concrete. A positive final displacement does not mean every part of the trip was in the positive direction.

We can check the chain in several ways. The net force and acceleration point the same way. Velocity changes by 6 m/s over three seconds at 2 m/s². The graph's signed areas agree with the displacement equation. Adding the initial position gives the correct final coordinate. If the force changed during the trip, this single constant-acceleration calculation would need to be divided into suitable intervals or replaced with a more detailed model.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, a forecast needs both its present motion and the forces changing that motion. Starting with force alone leaves out initial velocity and position. Connecting all three ideas gives us a prediction we can explain, check, and revise when new evidence arrives.

title: Build a prediction one coordinate at a time
subtitle: A two-dimensional plan with fixed axes and clear assumptions
paragraphs: A two-dimensional prediction can look complicated because the motion points at an angle. The solution becomes manageable when we keep one fixed frame and calculate each coordinate separately. I want the plan to show what was measured, what is being assumed, and how the result follows. Our probe example gives us a way to practice that reasoning.

Locate the probe’s starting point in Section C. It starts at (−20, 5) m and moves steadily at 10 m/s, directed 30° from the positive horizontal axis toward the positive vertical axis. We want its position after 2 s. The coordinates describe where it starts. The speed and angle describe its velocity. They do not describe the same thing, and the negative starting coordinate does not mean negative horizontal motion.

Resolve the velocity along the fixed axes. Because the angle begins at the positive horizontal axis, <eq><var>v</var><sub>x</sub> = <var>v</var> cos 30° = (10 m/s) cos 30° ≈ 8.66 m/s</eq>. The vertical component is <eq><var>v</var><sub>y</sub> = <var>v</var> sin 30° = 5.00 m/s</eq>. Both are positive. Using 10 m/s independently along each axis would invent a larger velocity than the one we were given.

Use the two steady-velocity equations in Section B, one for each coordinate: xf = x0 + vxt and yf = y0 + vyt. Both calculations use the same two seconds. Horizontally, xf = −20 m + (8.66 m/s)(2 s) ≈ −2.68 m. Vertically, yf = 5 m + (5 m/s)(2 s) = 15 m.

The predicted coordinates are therefore (−2.68, 15) m, using rounded horizontal components. The probe has moved rightward, yet remains left of the vertical axis. That is consistent: starting at −20 m and moving 17.32 m right does not quite reach zero. The blue start and end points on the notes page should tell the same story as those signed calculations.

Check the displacement components: <eq>Δ<var>x</var> ≈ +17.32 m</eq> and <eq>Δ<var>y</var> = +10 m</eq>. Their combined magnitude is approximately 20 m, matching a speed of 10 m/s maintained for two seconds. The displacement points in the same direction as the steady velocity. Agreement between the component calculation, diagram, and total travel is stronger evidence than a calculator result alone.

A complete plan also checks that all units match before substitution and that the chosen model fits the interval. If velocity changes, the two steady-velocity equations cannot describe the whole trip as written. If the starting measurements have uncertainty, the final coordinates should carry appropriate uncertainty too. More digits in the arithmetic do not create more precise measurements.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, treating Earth as fixed and velocity as steady are classroom simplifications. Real orbital predictions must account for changing gravitational effects and Earth's motion. Within our model, we can still make a defensible claim by naming the axes, future time, assumptions, and predicted coordinates, then asking whether both objects occupy the same place at the same time.

title: A good forecast can change with the evidence
subtitle: Defending a claim, comparing ranges, and explaining revision
paragraphs: A forecast is useful when someone else can follow the reasoning behind it. Giving a location without a time, reference frame, or uncertainty leaves too much unsaid. Today we bring those pieces together and examine what happens when a new measurement changes the result. Revising a prediction is part of using evidence responsibly.

Begin with the earlier constant-velocity model: xf = x0 + vt. The starting position was 8.0 ± 0.5 m, velocity was −2.0 ± 0.1 m/s, and elapsed time was exactly 3 s in the model. The central prediction was 8.0 m + (−2.0 m/s)(3 s) = 2.0 m. Its conservative uncertainty bound was 0.5 m + (3 s)(0.1 m/s) = 0.8 m, giving an interval from 1.2 m to 2.8 m.

Follow the revised forecast in Section D. A new measurement changes the velocity estimate to −1.5 ± 0.1 m/s. Keep the same starting-position estimate and exact elapsed time. The revised center is xf = 8.0 m + (−1.5 m/s)(3 s) = 3.5 m. The new velocity is less negative, so the predicted decrease in position is smaller. That sign check explains why the final position moves upward on the number line.

The center shifts by (0.5 m/s)(3 s) = +1.5 m. The uncertainty bound stays δxf = δx0 + tδv = 0.8 m, because the input bounds did not change. We now report xf = 3.5 ± 0.8 m, or 2.7 m to 4.3 m. The full interval is still 1.6 m wide. A changed center does not automatically mean a changed uncertainty.

Compare the three ranges on the same axis in Section C. The middle range shows an illustrative observed position of 3.5 ± 0.1 m, an interval from 3.4 m to 3.6 m. That observed interval does not overlap the earlier forecast, but lies within the revised forecast. The new prediction is consistent with this observation under the stated bounds. Agreement supports the model for this comparison; it does not prove that every assumption will remain valid at later times.

Keep the symbols distinct. Capital delta, Δ, means a change in a quantity. Lowercase delta, δ, labels an uncertainty bound here. We are adding the largest allowed contributions, not calculating a standard deviation or an impact probability. The range also does not automatically cover an omitted effect such as acceleration. A model error and an uncertain measurement are different reasons a prediction may need revision.

I want a defense of the forecast to connect four things: the claim, the evidence, the reasoning, and the limits. State the predicted position and time in a named frame; identify the measurements; explain the equation and assumptions; and show the allowed range. When revising, identify which input or assumption changed and trace its effect through the calculation.

For our fictional asteroid, 2026-XJ, this is the standard for reporting our conclusion. We can compare forecasts with observations and update them openly. The physics tells us what motion the model predicts; decisions about cost, feasibility, or a response require additional information. A clear forecast makes that later discussion better informed without claiming more certainty than the evidence provides.
